thread.title: Earnings Don't Matter? - SPDR S&P 500 Trust ETF (NYSEARCA:SPY)

author: Elazar Advisors, LLC
title: Earnings Don't Matter? - SPDR S&P 500 Trust ETF (NYSEARCA:SPY)
text:
The stock market is down huge and most of the blame was given to the Fed or the White House. But earnings are what triggered this downturn. We recommended subscribers be fully hedged since early October when we felt Q3 earnings season was going to be weak. And oh it was weak. Q4 earnings season starting in January should be worse. Stocks can turn up big when an earnings low is in sight. We're not there yet.
Tariffs Were Not News Until They Hit Earnings
Ahead of Q3 earnings season in early October ( Pay Wall ) we said this,
"I am concerned about tariff news affecting earnings reports so I don't think this is a season to take big bets."
The point is that there were tons of headlines all year. But when the stories finally affected earnings reports in Q3 stocks then took a hit. The market started dropping in unison with weaker earnings reports.
Shocked Nobody Focuses On Earnings
I see everybody blaming the Fed or the White House but those stories have not changed that much all year. The White House is constantly full of news. The Fed had been raising rates. But this time earnings growth rates finally slowed in Q3. That was what was new and what changed. Of course the Fed and the White House may have exacerbated things of late.
But if earnings were still strong in Q3 stocks probably could have held up. So while everybody's focused on everything else, why not focus on what drives the true change in stock prices, earnings.
What I'm shocked about is that the media and many investors including thousands of comments here on this platform don't first cite the Q3 earnings slowdown. That's probably what is most important to stock prices and people ignore that key piece of information instead listening to the media or investment bank noise.
Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) had a very weak Q4 guide. Apple's (NASDAQ: AAPL ) guide called for a big revenue slowdown in Q4. Texas Instruments (NASDAQ: TXN ), out of nowhere said business slowed across the board in all markets.
Stocks are valued based on the perceived trajectory of potential coming earnings streams. This quarter and next quarter, no matter what time frame, cause analysts and funds to adjust their forward earnings estimates.
Did you ever notice that stocks move big on earnings day? Why is that? Because the large market players get the quarterly report card to readjust their forward earnings estimates.
That adjustment causes swings in stocks as large funds adjust to higher or lower expected earnings trajectories based on what was just reported.
The largest of funds first and foremost care about what a company can earn. From that you can figure out where it should trade.
The simple glaring proof that stocks trade big up and down on earnings day should be reason enough to adopt a focus that earnings are the core market driver.
Good Company, Good Fundamentals
It's not enough to own a company because it's a "good company" or a company has "good fundamentals." These are broad generalizations that brokerage firms use to drive commissions to get people to buy stocks.
We don't fall in love with companies rather we fall in love with a company's earnings. Are earnings accelerating because of strong revenues and light expenses? Or are earnings slowing because of slowing revenues and building expenses? That's what drives stock prices. We're all here in the market, why not focus on its main driver?
When we model current and past results and extrapolate those results into the future, that's what can get us to love a stock. Positioning, strategy, moat, etc, are all nice, but to love a company you have to see it in the bottom line. That helped us avoid big downside in "good companies" in Apple, Micron (NASDAQ: MU ), Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA ) and many others. They are all great companies but the earnings growth rates slowed. That change drives selling pressure. In this case that selling pressure built to a crash.
Loving a company because of some other factor other than earnings can cause you to ignore focusing on the core driver to stock prices; earnings.
What's the measure of "good fundamentals?" It's a very broad term.
These are excuses that should not be used to own a stock in tough times.
The right question to ask is will the earnings and revenue growth rates continue to deteriorate or will they start to accelerate? Have we seen any change in those trends? For now many companies are seeing slowing trends so it's too early to get excited.
That's what will determine if large funds will start to step in and buy again. The largest of funds may dip their toe in the water but to buy-in big, they need to see a bottom in those slowing earnings growth rates.
"Two Things Drive Stock Prices, Earnings And Interest Rates"
One person who we follow out there who "gets it" is Jeremy Siegel (no relation to Chaim Siegel of Elazar). He was concerned in September and October about stocks having another swoon into year end.
Jeremy Siegel keeps things simple.
In his interview he said,
"Two things make up stock prices, earnings and interest rates."
He said that while predicting the coming market drop. That's after he was a long-time bull.
My subscribers know he's probably the only person's work I listen to and quote besides my own work. He keeps things very simple and that simple is what matters most to markets. Let's also keep things simple.
Interest rates can't always be predicted but we respect and follow their changes. Our focus is finding great earnings stories, but in that process we also discover negative trends like we saw in Q3 and see in Q4.
Stocks are valued based on their earnings. Those future earnings have to be discounted back at an underlying interest rate. As those interest rates rise they lower the discounted cash flow values of those future earnings. Those future values are what define stock prices.
The Fed may have finally decided to slow down the pace of rate hikes and adjust the pace of balance sheet reductions.
Still left on the menu is the other main dish, earnings.
Q4 Reports and Guidance
One reason that Siegel was worried earlier in the year is he thought that 2019 earnings estimates were too high yet the Fed was still raising rates.
The reason the Fed is forced to slow down their pace is because business trends are slowing.
Come January you still have company guidance risk as earnings season sets in. Companies will guide for Q1 and 2019.
Large investors have been selling into that.
Our caution going into Q3 based on tariffs and trade hitting earnings probably gets magnified in these Q4 reports.
We've spoken to multiple large-cap tech companies in the last few weeks. We think that Q4 is going to be tough. Many of our earnings estimates are below the Street, which is concerning. That means to us there's earnings risk.
By now you can agree that earnings risk is stock price risk.
If you think about it, what CEO would want to stick his or her neck out and make big business decisions with the stock market drop and US-China trade talks still up in the air. No CEO will want to take that risk right now.
So if you think about the domino of how cycles work, that would mean that those CEOs order a little bit less. Their suppliers then order less, on down the supply chain.
This 90 day negotiating period between Trump and Xi can likely compound slowing earnings growth rates in Q4 and likely will cause companies to need to lower Q1 and 2019 guidance.
Remember, other than interest rates, earnings drive stock prices. Stocks are valued based on their earnings potential.
A general drop in company guidance in January can help cause further risk for stocks.
A Note On Valuations
My subscribers know that I generally don't talk that much about valuations. Valuations don't drive stock prices. Earnings and earnings growth rates drive stock prices. If valuations are cheap or expensive, still the more important factor that drives stock price changes will be if earnings bottom, improve, slow, speed up, etc.
Buying because "stocks are cheap" is like buying because "it's a good company" or "good fundamentals."
Buying because stocks are cheap means that you need to wait for growth rates to bottom and turn back up. When does that happen? We don't know. We'd rather get some inkling of that happening first before we started buying in a bigger way.
Earnings Momentum Drives Stocks
The mover of stocks is when large funds pull the trigger. Most of those funds are earnings-momentum-driven and care very much about changes in earnings growth rates. Remember the example above of stocks making big moves on earnings day based on large funds adjusting?
So what matters more than valuations is the direction of earnings growth rates and if we're going to beat or miss earnings estimates. That causes large funds to adjust their forward outlook.
Look how the market moves are predicted by changes in earnings trajectories.
Source
Above you have the S&P 500 (NASDAQ: SPY ) chart versus its earnings trajectory. That shows you that when earnings (in orange) peak, stocks peak soon after and sometimes simultaneously.
Therefore listening carefully for changes in earnings trends can give you hugely important hints on the coming direction in stock prices.
Our caution going into Q3 and now Q4 was based primarily on our earnings work but also some technicals that just never turned positive for us.
Again, to make big bets, you want that orange line above to start picking back up, but if anything there's fear that it could be peaking.
Conclusion
We may get some bounces along the way but earnings saw a big slowdown in Q3. I expect Q4 and Q1 to see the same thing. To buy in a big way you need to sell yourself that Q2 and Q3 will start to see a re-acceleration in earnings growth rates. It's possible but we're only one quarter into a slowdown and I still think it's too early to take big bets on the long side. The earnings chart above also tells you, you don't have to predict. Why prognosticate earnings? You can see it happen to know if you have support. The market can soon follow.
